newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: India buys 120,000 tns diesel in tender for Oct.
newsitem.headline: India buys 120,000 tns diesel in tender for Oct.

text.p: State-owned Indian Oil Corp (IOC) bought only 120,000 tonnes of high speed diesel in three cargoes in its tender for October delivery, much lower than the lowest projection of 400,000 tonnes on Friday, traders said on Monday.

Traders believe that this could be IOC's lowest purchase by monthly tender in recent years and they expected the paper market to fall further after losing 30 cents a barrel on Friday on concerns of a low award.

The market was seen to be especially bearish since India bought only 255,000 tonnes of diesel for September and was initially expected to buy as much as 800,000-1.0 million tonnes for October to make up for the low September award.
Traders said Dutch trader Vitol was awarded two cargoes while Kuwaiti-based International Petroleum Group (IPG) had one cargo.
The awarded prices for the 0.5 percent sulphur diesel ranged between $1.98 and $2.00 per barrel above MidEast spot quotes on a cost-and-freight (c-and-f) to the Indian west coast.

Two cargoes will be delivered during the first 10 days in October--one 45,000-tonne cargo to Kandla and one 30,000-tonne cargo to Goa or Kandla. One 45,000-tonne cargo will be delivered during the second 10 days to Kandla, traders said.
They said the reason for the very low award could be because IOC could not decide how to implement the tender and might decide to issue a supplementary tender to make up for possible shortages.
Traders said said there appeared to be some conflicts between the Finance Ministry and the Oil Coordination Committee on the volume of oil products that IOC should buy.

While one party wanted to buy as much as 800,000 tonnes to meet India's demand, the other party was concerned with the port congestions, especially at Madras or Haldia, with cargoes being delayed for at least two months. India has to incur heavy demurrage costs because of this, traders said.
They said the paper market for September would be hit particularly hard by the low award as the market also has to contend with excess cargoes for that month.

Traders also noted that a further fall in prices could be limited by China's potential purchases. China's latent demand has been put on hold recently because of high prices which exceeded $25.50 a barrel on a fee-on-board Singapore basis.
But the price fall on Friday has already attracted Chinese buying.
Traders said China was heard to have purchased at least two prompt diesel cargoes on Friday at between $199.00 and $199.50 per tonne, c-and-f southern China.
China might buy more if prices fall under $25.00 per barrel fob basis, traders said.
